source: Hollan, Hutchins, Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Theory paper. Sets the unit of analysis as the whole functional system, not the skull. Names three kinds of distribution: across people, between internal and external structure, and through time.
numbers: No experiment of its own. Cites Kirsh and Maglio 1994 (Tetris epistemic actions) and cockpit studies without new numbers.
quote: Cognitive processes may be distributed across the members of a social group.
limits: It is a framing and method paper, so it gives no effect size. The core claim cannot be falsified in one test.
agent_relevance: Frame model plus program plus checks as one system and measure at system level.

source: Hollan, Hutchins, Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Authors admit the method, cognitive ethnography, is observational and its inferences are at times underconstrained by the data. They propose 'ethnographically natural' experiments to fill the gap.
numbers: No quantitative evidence offered for the theory itself.
limits: Evidence base for the founding theory is mostly case studies (ship navigation, cockpit). Few controlled tests.
agent_relevance: Do not treat the frame as proven. Use it as a design lens, then test each piece with ablation.

source: Hesselmann and Gollo (2020) No conclusive evidence for a Google Stroop effect. A replication study
finding: Replication of Sparrow, Liu and Wegner 2011, the best-known 'internet as external memory' lab effect. Built closer to the original after the original author criticised the 2018 failed replication. Still no effect.
numbers: N = 117 tested, sequential Bayes factor analysis on N = 89. BF01 = 5.07 favouring the null. Mean RT 825 ms (SD 453) general words vs 821 ms (SD 379) computer words in the hard-question condition.
limits: One German student sample. BF of 5 is moderate, not decisive. Only tests the priming claim, not offloading in general.
agent_relevance: The priming demonstration of the extended-memory story is weak. Do not rely on it as motivation.

source: Hesselmann and Gollo (2020) No conclusive evidence for a Google Stroop effect. A replication study
finding: The paper reports that Camerer et al. 2018 (large replicability project) already failed twice to replicate the Google Stroop effect. Original used N = 46; Camerer replication used N = 104 plus 130.
numbers: Original N = 46; Camerer N = 104 (+130); this study N = 117.
limits: Failure to replicate the Stroop priming does not refute that people do offload memory to devices. Other work is separate.
agent_relevance: Keep the theory but drop weak priming evidence from the case.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science
finding: Large replication project of 21 high-profile studies including Sparrow et al. 2011. About 13 of 21 replicated. Replicated effects were roughly half the original size. Sparrow Exp. 1 (Google Stroop) did not replicate.
numbers: Roughly 62% replicated in the direction of the original; mean effect about half original size (figures from memory, not opened this session).
limits: Not opened this session. Counts from memory. Treat as a lead, not verified numbers.
agent_relevance: Expect smaller effects than in founding papers.

source: Woolley et al. (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups
finding: Groups show a single general factor (c) that predicts performance across varied tasks. c was only weakly tied to average or maximum member IQ and tied to social sensitivity and equal turn-taking.
numbers: 192 groups, 699 people in two studies. First factor explains about 43% of variance (from memory).
limits: Not opened. Later work disputes parts of it (Credé and Howardson 2017 questioned the single factor; Bates and Gupta 2017 found c tracks member IQ). Read before use.
agent_relevance: Group-level ability is real but fragile as a single number. Do not build the agent on a c-factor claim.

source: Riedl, Kim, Gupta, Malone, Woolley (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups
finding: Meta-analysis across many group datasets. Collective intelligence is predicted by average member ability and by social perception more than by cohesion or motivation. Member ability still matters.
numbers: Numbers not read this session (page blocked, 403).
limits: Not opened. Recorded only as a pointer for the later pass.
agent_relevance: Group-level gains depend on member quality, so a weak model in a loop does not become strong by structure alone.

source: Ren and Argote (2011) Transactive memory systems 1985-2010
finding: Review of transactive memory research (Wegner). Groups with a shared map of who knows what do better, but the benefit depends on accuracy of the map and task fit.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Placeholder for follow-up; a 2019 meta-analysis on context factors exists.
agent_relevance: A routing table of which tool or check knows what is the agent version of this.

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett, Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD? Multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: Benchmarked debate protocols against single-agent prompting on medical and reasoning sets. Debate in default form does not reliably beat self-consistency or Medprompt, and costs more calls.
numbers: MedQA accuracy about 0.65 for best settings; Medprompt best overall; Multi-Persona about 7% worse than Medprompt in default form.
limits: GPT-3.5/4 era and open models. Results depend strongly on hyperparameters.
agent_relevance: Social distribution of reasoning across copies of one model is not a free gain. Test against the cheap baseline first.

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett, Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD? Multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: A single prompt knob, the agreement intensity (how willing agents are to agree), moved results a lot. Tuning it lifted Multi-Persona from worst protocol to best and gave +15% on a 376-question USMLE subset (SoM +5%, ChatEval hardly changed).
numbers: +15% Multi-Persona, +5% Society of Mind, 376 USMLE questions.
limits: Tuned on small subsets. Hyperparameters transferred GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 but not to Mixtral 8x7B.
agent_relevance: Moderator found: the amount of agreement in the group. Expose it as a parameter and tune per task.

source: Wang, Wang, Su, Tong, Song (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: are multi-agent discussions the key?
finding: Multi-agent discussion beat a single agent only when the single agent had no demonstration in its prompt. With a strong single prompt (task description plus worked example), a single agent matched the best discussion framework.
numbers: Tested on FOLIO-wiki and other reasoning sets with ChatGPT-3.5; table values not extracted here.
limits: GPT-3.5 only for main tables. A weaker model (Bard) improved when helped by stronger LLMs in mixed groups.
agent_relevance: Prompt quality is a confound. Match single-agent prompt strength before crediting the collective.

source: Wang, Wang, Su, Tong, Song (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: are multi-agent discussions the key?
finding: Discussion can turn a right single-agent answer into a wrong group answer. Two error types: judge mistakes and wrong-answer propagation. The MAD framework (agents told to disagree) was the weakest.
numbers: Qualitative error analysis on FOLIO-wiki; example in Fig. 4.
limits: Small error sample.
agent_relevance: The aggregation step is a failure point. A checker must verify the combination, not just each member.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail?
finding: Built MAST, a taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 groups (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification), from 1642 annotated traces of 7 multi-agent frameworks. Failure rates on the 7 systems ranged 41% to 86.7%.
numbers: Inter-annotator kappa 0.88; 150 traces for the taxonomy; modes: step repetition 15.7%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, not recognising completion 12.4%, disobeying task spec 11.8%.
limits: Mostly coding and math tasks; GPT-4, Claude 3, Qwen2.5, CodeLlama era; most traces annotated by an LLM judge.
agent_relevance: These are the failures of a distributed system: lost role, repeated steps, withheld info. List them as checks in the schema.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail?
finding: Simple role and workflow fixes helped but did not solve it. Giving the CEO agent the last word in ChatDev raised task success by 9.4%. Missing or wrong verification remains a main failure category.
numbers: +9.4% success in ChatDev case study.
limits: One framework, one case study.
agent_relevance: Structural fixes give single-digit gains. Verification is where the weight lies.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a science of scaling agent systems
finding: Largest controlled test of single vs multi-agent LLM systems: 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks, 5 architectures, 3 model families. Gains depend on the task, not on agent count. Range from +80.8% (decomposable finance) to -70.0% (sequential planning).
numbers: Cross-validated R2 = 0.373 (0.413 with capability metric). Best architecture predicted for 87% of held-out configurations. Finance: centralized 0.631 vs single 0.349.
limits: Fixed token budget across arms, which penalises multi-agent. Predictive model explains under half of variance.
agent_relevance: Distribution helps only when the task decomposes. Sequential reasoning should stay in one loop.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a science of scaling agent systems
finding: Capability ceiling: once a single agent scores above about 45%, adding agents gave negative returns. Tool-heavy tasks lost to coordination overhead.
numbers: Capability ceiling beta = -0.236 (p = 0.004); tool-coordination beta = -0.096 (p = 0.002). SWE-bench Verified single 0.522: hybrid -2.1%, centralized -3.1%, decentralized -5.4%, independent -14.9%.
limits: Correlational regression on 260 cells.
agent_relevance: For a strong base model, extra agents add cost. Prefer one agent plus external checks.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a science of scaling agent systems
finding: A centralised verification step contains error spread. Independent agents with no cross-check amplified errors 17.2 times. Centralised coordination held it to 4.4 times.
numbers: Error amplification 17.2x independent vs 4.4x centralized.
limits: Amplification measured from trace-level token analysis.
agent_relevance: Direct support for 'model plus checks as one system': the check is what matters.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a science of scaling agent systems
finding: Decentralised coordination helped only on parallel exploration (dynamic web navigation, +9.2%). All multi-agent variants hurt sequential planning (-39% to -70%).
numbers: Planning: -39% to -70%; web: +9.2% decentralised.
limits: One planning benchmark.
agent_relevance: Task shape is the moderator.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Self-correction with no outside signal does not help and often hurts. Reported gains came from using oracle labels to stop the loop. With an oracle, GPT-4 on HotpotQA went 49.0 to 59.0.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one round of intrinsic self-correction. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0 over two rounds. Oracle GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5.
limits: Single-model prompted self-correction in 2023 models.
agent_relevance: External information is what makes the loop a real second part of the system. A same-model check is not distribution.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Multi-agent debate was no better than self-consistency when the number of responses was equalised. Cost-matched baselines erase part of the claimed gain.
numbers: Comparison at equal response count; no single headline number extracted.
limits: Earlier-generation models.
agent_relevance: Always cost-match the baseline.

source: Kamoi, Zhang et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction
finding: Survey conclusion: no prior work shows success with feedback from prompted LLMs alone, except on tasks unusually suited to it. Self-correction works well with reliable external feedback and after large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Three conclusions; no pooled effect size.
quote: self-correction works well in tasks that can use reliable external feedback
limits: Survey, not a meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Put reliable external checks (tests, code, retrieval) in the loop.

source: Gao et al. (2023) PAL: Program-aided language models
finding: Model writes a program and an interpreter runs it. This offloads the calculation to an external tool and beat chain-of-thought with the same model.
numbers: GSM8K 72.0 PAL vs 65.6 CoT (Codex); about +15 points above PaLM-540B CoT. GSM-HARD 61.2 PAL vs 23.1 CoT.
limits: Math word problems. Gain shrinks when the model already computes well.
agent_relevance: Cleanest case of model plus program as one system. The program carries the part the model does badly.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum, Mordatch (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning through multiagent debate
finding: Several model copies answer, read each other, and revise. Beats a single answer and plain self-reflection on arithmetic, GSM8K, chess, MMLU and biographies. Arithmetic accuracy rose with number of agents.
numbers: Figures and tables only; exact values not extracted. Reflection gave a modest boost, debate a larger one.
limits: Later cost-matched work (Huang 2024, Smit 2024, Wang 2024) finds much of this gain shrinks against self-consistency.
agent_relevance: Original source of the society-of-minds claim. Treat as contested.

source: Li et al. (2024) More agents is all you need
finding: Plain sampling and voting over many copies raises accuracy with ensemble size, and the gain grows with task difficulty. No debate needed.
numbers: GSM8K +12 to +24 points; MATH +6 to +10; MMLU +5 to +11; HumanEval +4 to +9; Chess +1 to +4. Llama2-13B at 59% on GSM8K matched Llama2-70B.
limits: Voting needs answers that can be compared; gain is smaller on easy tasks.
agent_relevance: The cheap baseline that most collective claims must beat.

source: Riedl (2026, ICLR) Emergent coordination in multi-agent language models
finding: Information-theory test for real group-level structure in LLM teams doing a guessing game. Prompts change the type of coordination: a persona gives stable differences; persona plus 'think about what others might do' gives complementary roles.
numbers: Success rates in the table include 53%, 59%, 61% (Llama-3.1-70B) and 5.5% (Llama-3.1-8B, ToM prompt); column mapping partly unclear from text extraction.
limits: Does not claim team beats solo. The small Llama-3.1-8B showed no gain, likely low theory-of-mind ability. Simple task.
agent_relevance: Role and theory-of-mind prompts change group behaviour, but the base model must be able to use them.
